content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers the problem of probabilistic hierarchical forecasting where the goal is to generate coherent probabilistic predictions for a large number of time series arranged in a hierarchical structure. Specifically, a new top-down approach to hierarchical forecasting is proposed. An attention-based RNN model is used to learn the distribution of the proportions, which are then coupled with an independent univariate probabilistic forecasting model for the root time series. Experiments on several public datasets show signiﬁcant improvements on most datasets compared to state-of-the-art methods. The authors also provide a theoretical justiﬁcation of the top-down approach compared to bottom-up methods (in an idealized setting).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- Probabilistic forecasting for hierarchical time series is a challenging and important research problem for many applications.
- The proposed method can be used with any forecasting method for the root time series, and generates coherent probabilistic forecasts by construction. 
- The authors compare their method with multiple baselines and datasets.
- A theoretical analysis is provided to justify the advantage of a top-down approach over a bottom-up method


Weaknesses

- The paper is poorly written (see comments). The terminology is not properly introduced, e.g. "probabilistic, hierarchically-coherent models", coherent probabilistic forecasts", "revised coherent forecasts", "the samples are reconciled", "root time series", "hierarchy tree", "leaf forecasts", "child", "same family", etc.

- It is not clear how the theoretical analysis relates to the proposed method. It seems that it motivates the top-down method over a bottom-up approach in an idealized setting, which is not new. Also, the authors should clearly discuss the assumptions and limitations of their analysis. For example, what is really analyzed is a method based on historical proportions.

- Experiments
	- It is not clear if the comparison between methods is fair. For example, how did you generate probabilistic forecasts from methods than only generate point forecasts?
	- "Note: Some of the baselines listed in Sec. 5 returned invalid quantiles (NaNs) and were omitted from the table."
		- Removing methods because they returned NaNs is not the best approach when comparing baselines. Why did they return NaNs? Also, is that the only reason why some methods do not appear for some datasets?

- Except for a "small" improvement in forecast accuracy, the methodological contribution of the paper is weak.

- The "related work" should clearly separate the literature on point and probabilistic forecasting. Furthermore, an important paper on "probabilistic hierarchical forecasting" is missing in the related work: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0377221722006087

Comments
- The authors talk about "coherent probabilistic forecasts", but do not define this concept.
- "Furthermore, none of these approaches can directly handle probabilistic forecasts."
	-> I disagree with this statement. The MinT approach provides coherent means and covariance matrix for the entire hierarchy, which enables probabilistic forecasting.
- In the introduction, it is stated that the parameters are obtained using an RNN, but later, the authors talk about an LSTM.
- y_hat and b_hat are not defined
- "The distribution of the future f(Y_F)"
	-> According to the paper, Y_F is an F x N matrix, and your goal is to predict, f, its density. However, this is not what your method is doing. The "coherency" paragraph in Section 2 is not clear.

- Typos: "each of row", "data distribution data", "an results"
- "Note that we only need to load all the time series of a given family into a batch."
	-> Why is that the case?

- Did you mean x_t (instead of x_i) in Section 4?
- Theta_i^b = p_i = theta_hat. Did you mean theta_0^t?

- What do you mean by "predictive distribution quantiles"?

- Their approach did not complete training within 2 weeks
	-> what kind of computer architecture did you use?

- In expression (3), you use Q_s^i but you only defined Q_F^i.

- Did you average the forecast error over the entire forecast horizon? This should be discussed in the text.

- What is p50?

- Section 4 and appendix
	-> i goes from t to n, then i goes from t to n, and in the appendix, i goes from 1 to n.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is hard to read and clearly lacks clarity and quality.

While the paper proposes a new top-down method, it is not clear how it advances the state-of-the-art given that there are other end-to-end probabilistic forecasting methods that are as general as the proposed method.

The authors did not discuss reproducibility. It is not clear whether they plan to provide the code associated with their paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: A major weakness of the paper is the lack of clarity, which makes the paper hard to read. Except for a "small" improvement in forecast accuracy, the methodological contribution of the paper is also weak. On the positive side, the authors compare their method with multiple baselines and datasets and show better forecast accuracy. A theoretical justification of the top-down method is also provided.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new technique for hierarchical coherence time series forecasting. The proposed technique takes a top-down approach by taking coarse sequences as parent nodes and fine-grained time stamps as children nodes, forming a hierarchical structure. The parent embedding and children embedding is jointed trained through LSTM and the parent nodes are passed through multihead attention. They also use a Dirichlet distribution in the loss function to capture the hierarchical structure.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
1. Time series forecasting is an important problem. 

Weakness: 
1. I don't see capturing hierarchical coherence has obvious benefits compared to prediction in high resolution and aggregates to low resolution. 
2. Using constraints to learn consistency is not very new. 
3. The justification for OLS is too simplified. 
4. Major baseline such as N-BEATS is not compared.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is not very clearly written and many important details are missing. The experiential design is lacking intuition.  The novelty is very high. The authors attached their source code as supplement material.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper proposes a new technique for hierarchical coherence time series forecasting. However, I have the following concerns: 

1. I know this is not a first work on temporal coherience, but I don't get the point of this tree structure and capturing hierarchical coherence -- I don't see obvious benefits compared to prediction in high resolution and aggregates to low resolution. It will be naturally consistent. 
2.  Structure and tree structure do not always hold. The authors never considered noisy time series, there could be a lot noise in real-world data such as sensor data. 
3. The authors claim that temporal consistency through matrix is novel and main contribution, but [1] has already use matrix constraint on time series to enforce temporal consistency. In addition, there is no  information about how many leafs per node. Is it equal to the prediction horizon = 35? 
4. The paper did not mention how large the temperal dependency window S could go with? In my experience, this kind of matrix constraint would only works in a short sequence. 
5. Is your parent node/simplex considering *overlapping* subsequences? How do you consider the correlated structure? 
6. On the loss function, I am not sure what the Dirichlet trying to learn. Are we trying to learn which child node to enforce your consistency here? In other word, S is learnt? There is nothing in the main body text talking about it except the figure. The inference part is also completely omitted. I am not seeing it in the main body.
7. I don't see any experiment designed to demonstrate the superior in hierarchical structure other than it is better in overall loss. It is certainly not intuitive. 
8. The paper used muti head attention. Thus, it is not supprised that the paper has better results than models like DeepAR. More recent baselines on transformers as well as N-Beats should be compared. 

Overall, although this paper works on an important problem, I am afraid that the paper is not sufficiently well written. Due to the writing and missing some baselines, the technical contribution is difficult to evaluate. I would suggest a reject. 

[1] Toeplitz Inverse Covariance-Based Clustering of Multivariate Time Series Data
David Hallac (Stanford University);Sagar Vare (Stanford University);Stephen Boyd (Stanford University);Jure Leskovec (Stanford University)

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a new approach to hierarchical, probabilistic forecasting that is based on modeling the proportions of children time series in the hierarchy with a temporal neural net model, rather than the time series values themselves.  In this way a simple time series model can be used to model the root level time series (which is typically more predictable and having clear time series characteristics such as predictable trend and clear seasonal pattern), and then the proportions of the children series can be predicted from the neural net model to disaggregate the root level forecast in a top down model.  Additionally, a distribution over proportions is directly modeled to enable probabilistic forecasting.

The authors also prove for one particular case of a hierarchical time series with values generated top-down, that the top-down based forecasting approach can have significantly less risk than a bottom-up forecast approach.

Finally, the authors compare their proposed neural-net-based top-down forecast approach to a large set of different baselines on multiple hierarchical time series datasets, showing consistently superior performance, along with reporting some results for variations of the model (different root level forecasters).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The approach is interesting and novel.  Although I am aware of one other similar proportion model learning approach (see below) - it is using a much less flexible share / proportion model (multinomial model) and not neural nets, and also as a result does not directly enable these proportions to evolve over time, as is done in this paper by using temporal neural nets - and also does not consider probabilistic forecasting.  This is the first such approach I am aware of using neural nets to do this, and is something that makes a lot of sense and good to see the results of applying - so it is definitely useful to the forecasting field.

"Demand Modeling in the Presence of Unobserved Lost Sales" Subramanian and Harsha  


2. It makes a lot of sense to use proportions for many different advantages - which actually the authors don't even list all of these advantages in the paper:
    -  Using proportions automatically normalizes the series (facilitating cross series and transfer learning as well) - as a time series of proportions will always be between 0 and 1 - so this could make different time series more comparable and able to apply the same model across them effectively / learn common patterns across different series and families of series.
    - Using proportions as is done here enables efficient batch SGD training - since, unlike general multivariate forecast model training where all time series must be passed to each example in a batch to perform SGD and update parameters, in this case only time series in the same family need to be included in an update for a batch.  So as long as there is sufficient hierarchy defined for the time series - this is much more scalable and could scale to larger number of series.  It's a pity that the computational complexity and run times weren't analyzed at all as it would be interesting to compare to multivariate methods and demonstrate this aspect (and applicability of distributed training).
    - As mentioned this approach enables fully exploiting the properties of predictability at the most aggregate level. 


3. The experimental study is extensive - with many methods compared against and multiple datasets, and additional details in the appendix.



Weaknesses:

1. There are general weaknesses / limitations of the proposed approach.  In particular 2 come to mind:
    - a) The root-level model can't be informed / benefit from base level forecasts / knowledge - and similar bottom-up information flow is not possible.  I.e., just as there can be an assumption that better top level forecasts can benefit lower levels, there is also an argument that in some datasets bottom-level forecasts could help inform upper-level forecasts / summarize granular information to inform aggregate level forecasts.  One might argue for an alternative model where the root level model is part of the model as well and fit in an end-to-end fashion along with the proportion model (as is done in the above mentioned paper as well).
    - b) Related to the above, the subsequent bottom-level forecasts have no way of adapting to error in the top-level forecast.  I.e., this approach (as with all top-down approaches) is very heavily dependent on an accurate top level model.  If this model is not highly accurate, the base level models will only get worse in lower levels with error propagation and no hope of correction as the model is trained on the actual proportions and is purely top-down.  It would be interesting to see more analyses around the impact of inaccurate root level models - such as showing the overall error increase as less and less accurate root models are used.

2. Experiments could still be improved.  In particular, it would be best and useful to see the best, state of the art forecast results with bottom-up aggregation, to see how much if any is the gap - as there have been a large number of forecast methods out-performing the baselines used in the results (DeepAR and DeepSSM) in the past few years.  Additionally for the case of M5 it would be nice to see how these results compare with the winning probabilistic forecasting method of the competition.  

Some experiments, especially for abalation study / comparing different variations seem incomplete - as they are only performed on one dataset - and it would be best to include results on all datasets in the appendix.  E.g.,  showing results of TDProb with different root models only for wiki2 - should show it for other datasets as well.  Similarly, for showing other metric results - it's also only for one dataset in the appendix.

Additionally, the results on L0 for TDProb vs. prophet are confusing.  Why does L0 have variance for TDProb but not prophet? As I'm assuming L0 is the root, these should be identical in all runs.



3. It would be good to see runtime and complexity analysis / results.


4. Model specifics could be better described.  Especially given some typos making it harder to follow - e.g., "Note that the attention is only applied across the third dimension i.e across the children" - this seems like a typo - the third dimension is the embedding dimension as stated earlier, the second dimension is the children dimension.

It would be better to explicitly write out the equation for applying the attention and getting the final weights - I feel Equations (1) and (2) could be combined to make more space, and "MF ←MultiHeadAttg,l(DF)," could for example be replaced with the actual mathematical equation.  


5. There are unsupported / inaccurate statements made in the introduction:

It is stated (about many existing hierarchical forecasting approaches):
"These approaches are usually disadvantaged in terms of using the hierarchical constraints only as a post-processing step, and not during generation of the base forecasts. Furthermore, none of these approaches can directly handle probabilistic forecasts."

For the first part, some methods do incorporate hierarchy in generating the base forecasts / learning the model.  However, even for those that don't, such as post-forecast reconciliation approaches, why are they disadvantaged?   Some citation should be provided to support this claim or reasonable explanation here why this is the case.  Personally I feel in some cases an argument could be made they won't be as effective as directly factoring in the hierarchical relationships in the forecast modeling itself, but there are also cases where independent forecasting followed by reconciliation could be just as effective or even more effective.

For the second part, it seems all of these reconciliation approaches actually can be applied to probabilistic forecasts.  In particular, a simple universal approach is to sample from the probabilistic forecast, and reconcile the samples.  The reconciled samples then provide the new (reconciled) characterization of the probabilistic forecast - as any statistics of the distribution can be extracted from this set of reconciled samples (such as prediction intervals).  At least this is an approach to enable applying any of these methods to probabilistic forecasts, and it should be explained why this is not sufficient.  In fact, after reading the paper I see the authors essentially take the same approach for their proposed method - so it seems this approach can hardly be discounted.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper and model development is mostly easy to follow and understand.  The paper is of good quality - well positioned in related work, well organized, soundly developed.  The approach is a novel and useful one.  Details and procedures for experiments are clearly explained and code is provided, so reproducibility should not be an issue.

There are a few minor grammar issues and awkward phrasing, e.g.: "...parameters of the Dirichlet distribution for each family is obtained..." (should be "...are obtained...").
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall while I feel like the paper could be improved further and the proposed method does have some limitations, overall it's an interesting, novel, and useful approach and set of results - and defines a useful and effective way of doing forecasting for hierarchical time series improving on some simpler approaches and commonly used paradigms in a meaningful way.  I.e., enabling a more effective and flexible alternative to past top-down forecasting approaches if nothing else.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a deep top-down approach to hierarchical time series forecasting. The distribution of proportions of child time series over its parents is forecasted. An independent univariate probabilistic forecasting for the root time series is conducted. The resulting forecasting results are coherent naturally. On most datasets, the proposed method achieves significant performance improvements.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: Overall, the paper is more like a practical one than a methodological or theoretical one. The main contribution is forecasting proportions instead of the original time series. The forecasting for the root time series can be coupled and coherent probabilistic forecasts can be obtained naturally. The architecture includes the popular LSTM and self-attention, which lacks novelty.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is written well, and I have no concerns about the quality and reproducibility. The only concern is the lack of methodological novelty, making the contribution not enough.

Some questions:
i) in Inference, authors use sampling to obtain the final children forecasts by combining the forecasts of the root model and children proportions. Can this be done analytically? Because you have the distributions of both root time series and children proportions, the target here is the product of two random variables. It may be feasible to obtain an analytical solution, the sampling-based solution is not optimal.

ii) In DirLL loss function, the normalization constant $B(\alpha)$ is a multivariate beta function. How to numerically deal with it efficiently?
content.summary_of_the_review: As I pay more attention to the methodological contribution, my recommendation may be biased and not comprehensive. Other reviewers can provide different opinions from different perspectives.
